newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - Creditanstalt sale thrown open.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Creditanstalt sale thrown open.

text.p: The race for Austrian sell-off candidate Creditanstalt appeared wide open again on Monday after Finance Minister Viktor Klima hinted he was less than happy with a lone bid for the country's number two bank.

Austrian media were abuzz with speculation over Klima's next move in the six-year long privatisation after he indicated on Sunday an eleventh-hour offer by the Austro-Italian-German consortium around insurer EA-Generali for the government's 70 percent voting stake in the country's number two bank was too vague.

The group, headed by EA-Generali and including Germany's Commerzbank and Banca Commerciale Italiana, on Friday said it had made an offer for the government's stake in Creditanstalt-Bankverein just hours before a midnight deadline expired.

Italian-controlled EA-Generali on Friday said its proposal was an "updated version" of a bid the group originally made last October, when it offered to pay nine billion schillings ($858 million) for about two thirds of the government's Creditanstalt stake and sell the remaining shares in a secondary offering.
No details of the new offer were made public, and it was not immediately clear whether the consortium bid was for all or just parts of the government's stake.

Klima, in charge of the sale, on Sunday said he wanted to see more information on how many of the government's 19.9 million ordinary Creditanstalt shares each of the consortium members proposed to acquire.

A spokesman for Klima on Monday said the minister and his advisors, investment bank JP Morgan, were still scrutinising the consortium's offer. Klima is expected to report his findings at the weekly cabinet meeting on Tuesday.

Savings bank Die Erste, which left the consortium on Friday after frantic negotiations failed to bridge a growing rift between its members, poured oil on the fire by saying it was still hoping for a lead role in what has become Austria's longest-running privatisation drama.
"We're watching the affair with great interest," Die Erste board spokesman Michael Ikrath told Reuters. "Our interest in playing a role (in the privatisation) remains unchanged."

Speculation in Wednesday's edition of daily Kurier that Die Erste was now trying to form a new consortium of bidders and had approached Germany's Allianz to work on a competing bid could not immediately be verified.

Klima has threatened to reopen the bidding process to other potential buyers if the consortium's bid, the only known offer so far, failed to meet his demands. The government has repeatedly said it wants to sell its entire stake for cash.
A study by JP Morgan last year valued the government's holding in the flagship bank at around 18 billion schillings.

A number of foreign companies, among them Allianz and CS Holding of Switzerland, over the past years have lost interest in the bank after becoming frustrated with Austrian politics and the government's apparent desire to keep the country's most traditional bank in domestic hands.

Those attempts were dealt a serious blow when Die Erste split with its erstwhile partners over its proposal to form a joint venture with Creditanstalt, which it would control, with the expressed purpose of "safeguarding Austrian interests".
That plan irritated the other members of the consortium, since Die Erste is barely a third of the size of Creditanstalt, which has total assets of almost 700 billion schillings.

"The (consortium's) offer neither helps to improve the structure of the Austrian banking sector nor does it safeguard Austrian interests," Die Erste's Ikrath said. "But apparently Klima himself has some doubts about that, too." ($1=10.49 Schilling)
